wa_j_tnar.notes: Approach pitch; moderate free climbing to establish first belay on the wall
130 feet; easy free climbing up small ramp to left, steep cracks to large ledge, then thin aid on face to stance below splitter crack
80 feet; splitter cracks to sheltered slabby belay; excellent portaledge bivy site
120 feet; crux aid pitch - A3 up left-facing crack with roof halfway up, hook doom block, exit corner right past hooks to stance below mud corner
Varied climbing with water seepage risk; afternoon waterfall conditions common
Continued aid climbing with water seepage; often running water in spring/early summer
130 feet; left-facing corner on rivets to steep crack series overhanging 40+ feet; fixed line recommended for descent
150 feet; A2 from belay, C1 up beautiful splitter hand crack through overhang (5.10), 5.9 free climbing to belay - classic pitch
140 feet; second aid crux - right of bush quest on thin pins, rivets, hooks; bat hooks bypass chossy corner; long reach to beaks near top at bolt (tension traverse or reach)
Mixed climbing transitioning to upper wall pitches
Continued aid with improving rock quality
Easier aid climbing as route approaches summit section
Further aid climbing with reducing difficulty
Upper pitches include traverse left to large right-facing corner with 5.10 or C1 root aiding, and a 5.7 mossy dihedral and gully to summit - deteriorating rock quality near finish

wa_the_tiger.notes: Easy scrambling moves past flakes and a pruned tree, about 8 m up, gain a clean, slabby left-facing corner that leads to a two-bolt anchor. Do not follow the gully to its highest ledge, the one that splits the wall at half height: it leads to the start of P4 instead.

A few metres up the corner, make awkward moves over the roof onto the golden slab above. Zigzag past bolts, first left on crack features and then back right, pull a bulge, and follow thin crack features up and left. The moves after the bulge are thin and sustained; easier ground leads to the anchor. Graded 5.10+ to 5.10d.

Up the left-facing corner past flakes and a bolt, then step right to a second bolt and pull into the upper left-facing corner. Sustained and technical with finicky gear, to a two-bolt anchor at a large ledge. Walk the belay left 10–15 m along the ledge to a cairn at the start of P4. Given as 5.11 to 5.11c.
Another left-facing, slabby corner to a bolt, then face moves right past steep, flexing flakes and a solid layback flake. Pull around the arete to the right to the anchor.
A thin, technical finger corner leads into the big cave, Tiger Belly's Lair; the anchor is on the right side of the cave. Sustained and stout for its grade, which is given from 5.11- to 5.11a.

Traverse right out of the cave, clip a bolt, and climb a steep wall on positive holds, trending slightly right to a stance below the leaning roof. The Eye of the Tiger variation (5.12c/5.12+) climbs the orange corner straight out of the cave for about 40 m and rejoins the route above; accounts differ on whether it rejoins after P7 or P8.

The crux: follow the exposed, stepped roof leftward past two bolts, alternating strenuous underclings with holds above the lip. At the end of the roof (a BD #2 fits), reachy but easier moves past a pin reach the anchor. Grades given are 5.12- to 5.12b.

A short, steep, strenuous layback in the left-facing corner past a fixed piece and two bolts, then a rest on a stance. From a bolt, hand-traverse left past another bolt, with poor feet at first, onto the slab and a sloping belay. A second two-bolt anchor about 7 m up and right is off route.

Straight up cracks and flakes until you can trend left on twin thin cracks, balancy and protected by two fixed nuts. An easier ramp leads left to the anchor at the base of the Tiger Flake. Given as 5.11 to 5.11b.

Clip the bolt left of the anchor and make committing moves to a small ledge, then undercling and jam left around the giant Tiger Flake and continue to its final steep, wide section. Keep a BD #5 for after the first section, to protect the follower, and a #6 for the end. Manage the rope carefully; belay on a big ledge.

Broken cracks and blocky features lead up and right to a final bulge and onto the ridge; anchor from a tree. The weakest pitch on the route. Descend by rappelling the route with two ropes, including diagonal rappels, or by the third-class ramp on the left side of the wall.

wa_cutthroat_south_buttress.notes: Ropes up about 100 ft below where the approach gully forks; climbs the gully's left side up to the ridge crest, then heads left along the crest to a tree belay.
Follows the ridge crest staying right of the steeper faces, then breaks left up an obvious ramp to a huge ledge.
Either stays on the blocky crest or traverses left on 4th/5th-class terrain via a gully/ramp; grainy, friable rock low down gives way to cleaner slab where some parties switch to approach shoes.

Threads a notch, then an awkward slabby traverse with big exposure on the right to a small ledge system; belays at the base of a chimney on rock several parties call the most questionable on the route.
Climbs the chimney onto the face and eases into a sandy ramp; crawl under a large chockstone (a reliable on-route landmark) before bouldering up to the belay.
Traverses ledges right off the belay then climbs cracks and flakes (a squeeze-chimney option exists); widely reported as the most enjoyable pitch on the route and nearly a full ropelength.
Fun, sustained laybacking and jamming up short steps to a small belay notch directly below the route's technical crux.

The crux pitch: climbs a ramp into a wide chimney/stembox with limited protection, steps right onto a cracked face, then makes an awkward left move into a sandy gully; a variant right of the true line adds a harder, off-route overhanging lieback.
Downclimbs a short notch, traverses a loose gully, then climbs a face to gain the upper gully leading toward the false summit.
Climbs a corner and a slabby lieback boulder problem to a short offwidth crack (a #4 cam protects it well); tops out near the false summit with reachy, bouldery moves.
A short downclimb off the false summit followed by easy face climbing across to the base of the final headwall, matching the route's described dip before its last push to the true summit.
The final airy pitch to Cutthroat's true summit (8,065 ft); exposed but moderate, after which most parties transition straight into the West Ridge or reversed-buttress descent.

wa_cutthroat_the_swarm.notes: Scramble 4th class on the right side of the prominent ledge system, traverse left to a smaller ledge, then climb the obvious left-facing dihedral through two small roofs. Belay on gear in a horizontal crack.

Move right over loose blocks, taking care not to drop them on anyone below, into 4th-class ground. This reaches the large treed ledge at the base of the headwall, with plenty of gear and tree belay options.

The standout pitch. The crux is the first 25 ft, a left-facing dihedral; extend the last piece with a long sling. Downclimb slightly left to a splitter finger crack that widens to hands and gets easier. Where it pinches out, a second crack starts 4 ft right. Follow it to a bolted anchor on a small stance. No protection bolts.

Climb hollow rock below a roof and place gear carefully, then move left to a pedestal, up the left-facing dihedral, and exit right. Belay at the bolted anchor next to a dead tree on a large flat ledge.
Start up the corner, then move right onto flared cracks that cross the face. The cracks steepen into an obvious short crux before a bolted anchor at a rest. Harder than it looks from below.

The hardest moves of the route: jamming and stemming up a demanding dihedral. Plug a 0.75 cam in a pod, span hard out left to a good edge, and clip the route's only protection bolt on the left wall. Bolted anchor.
Climb easy blocky ground, traverse about 20 ft right into a chimney, exit onto a ledge, then traverse about 15 ft left. Climb a short seam on small gear to a large ledge with a tree and a cave.

Exit through the keyhole at the top of the cave. The ground eases steadily to 4th class and scrambling. Belay on the ridge top, then descend via the South Buttress, or via the West Ridge if the buttress is busy.

wa_southwest_buttress.notes: A full rope-length up a corner then slightly right; mostly 5.6 climbing with one committing 5.7/5.8 move near the top. Build the anchor on gear (cams to 3 inches) in a crack.
Continue up and right to a small plateau; the belay is built on 0.5-1 inch cams or a few nut placements.
A short class-4 gully scramble gives way to a rising traverse up and left to a comfortable ledge; belay on 1-2 inch cam and nut placements.
A half-rope-length pitch trending left to gain the ridge crest — staying left is important, since climbing right leads into an unwanted 5.10 overhang.

The route's variation crux: a sustained corner past sections of loose rock with limited protection, per multiple trip reports. The standard (non-variation) line instead follows easier low-5th-class ridge scrambling to the same flat shelf.
Climb a right-leaning crack, then continue straight up a wall on good holds; belay off gear near the top of the ridge.
Follow the ridge crest, then traverse left to a wide crack between slabs; the belay is a sling backed up in a notch.
Choose between a loose gully with a chockstone or a rightward line up the wall toward the summit-ridge crack; both options top out near the same point below the final ridge.
A short final traverse along the summit ridge — the same terrain shared with the upper Northwest Ridge — leads to the narrow, exposed high point.
